name: Parsley and mint chewing
lead: Chewing fresh parsley or mint leaves is a folk method for freshening breath, often after garlic- or onion-heavy meals. People use it to avoid bad breath, which is one of the things that affects how close and approachable a person seems in conversation. Parsley is widely used as a garnish and is described on Wikipedia as being credited in cooking with neutralising garlic odours.[1]

Research is limited. A 2016 Journal of Food Science study by Rita Mirondo and Sheryl Barringer of Ohio State University had participants chew garlic and then consume foods; raw mint leaves deodorised measured breath volatiles more effectively than raw apple or raw lettuce, which cut volatiles by 50 percent or more for the first 30 minutes. The report did not mention parsley.[4] Wikipedia's halitosis article reports that evidence does not support dietary changes or chewing gum for bad breath in general.[2]

Bad breath has several causes; most genuine cases originate in the mouth, especially bacteria at the back of the tongue producing volatile sulfur compounds, while garlic and onion are temporary food-related contributors.[2]
infobox: Mirondo and Barringer, 2016, Journal of Food Science[4]

paras: Curly-leaf parsley is commonly served as a garnish on dishes such as potatoes, fish and steak, and parsley is a key ingredient in tabbouleh, falafel and salsa verde.[1] Peppermint and spearmint oils are common sources of mint flavour in confectionery.[3]

In the Ohio State experiment, participants chewed 3 grams of softneck garlic for 25 seconds and then consumed water or a test food, with breath volatiles measured by mass spectrometry. Raw apple and raw lettuce cut volatiles by 50 percent or more for the first 30 minutes, and raw mint leaves were more effective than either for every compound measured. Mint juice and heated foods also reduced volatiles, but less effectively, and green tea had no deodorising effect.[4] The researchers proposed that enzymes in raw foods and phenolic compounds destroy the odour compounds.[4]

The halitosis literature summarised on Wikipedia describes tongue cleaning and some mouthwashes as having tentative evidence, and says that evidence does not support dietary changes or chewing gum.[2]

Wikipedia notes normal culinary amounts of parsley are considered safe, while parsley seeds contain apiole and very large amounts may have uterotonic effects, so pregnant women are advised to avoid excess.[1] Peppermint may relax the lower oesophageal sphincter and aggravate reflux.[3]
No studies found on parsley for breath. For mint, the 2016 garlic-breath experiment found that chewing raw mint leaves reduced garlic breath volatiles in participants.[4]

Leaf chewing is described in lifestyle discussions as a cheap, food-based alternative to gum or mints. On T Nation, a poster on a low-carbohydrate fasting plan asked whether anyone had tried chewing parsley or mint leaves to deal with bad breath.[5]

lore.intro: Herb chewing is passed on as common-sense kitchen lore and appears occasionally on fitness forums, often among people on low-carbohydrate or high-protein diets who report breath changes.[5]

claims.claim: Chewing parsley or mint removes garlic breath.
claims.believers: Proponents say fresh herbs neutralise strong food odours; the chlorophyll in parsley is often cited as the reason.[5]
claims.experts: A 2016 study found raw mint leaves reduced garlic breath volatiles more than raw apple or lettuce for the first 30 minutes; parsley was not tested in the report.[4] Wikipedia's halitosis article says evidence does not support dietary changes or chewing gum in general.[2]

card.summary: Folk habit of chewing fresh herbs for fresh breath; untested in trials.
card.note: No studies; effect, if any, is brief.

quick.overview:
Some people chew fresh parsley or mint after meals to freshen breath.

No clinical studies were found, and sources describe such remedies as at most short-term masking.
quick.mechanism: Fresh herb flavour and chewing-induced saliva may cover odour briefly.
quick.risks: Low in food amounts; peppermint can aggravate reflux and parsley seeds are not recommended in pregnancy.

chain: Chew fresh parsley or mint leaves
Fresh flavour and plant compounds act on food odour compounds
Fresher breath for a short time
angle.text: People chew parsley or mint leaves after meals to reduce garlic or onion breath and have fresher breath around others. The effect studied for mint in a garlic experiment lasted for the measured period of about half an hour.
